content: The proportion of individuals diagnosed with chronic hepatitis C (HCV viraemic infection) is calculated from the estimated population with hepatitis C. Among those diagnosed with chronic hepatitis C, the proportion of individuals assessed for treatment eligibility is determined using non-invasive tests for staging, such as the APRI score and ALT levels. The proportion of individuals diagnosed with chronic hepatitis C who initiate treatment is also measured. Additionally, the proportion of individuals initiating treatment who undergo an HCV viral load test as a test of cure (sustained virological response at week 12) is assessed. Finally, the proportion of individuals initiating treatment and achieving sustained virological response at week 12 is calculated. At the initial stage of a program, the cascade of care may be estimated using ad hoc mechanisms, such as surveys, treatment cohorts from tertiary hospital data, and medicine sales data. However, the optimal approach to monitoring a national program for hepatitis B and C testing and treatment involves establishing a patient-centered data monitoring system. This system should integrate these services into the broader governance framework of the national health management information system. At global, regional, or country levels, the cascade of care is ideally presented in relation to the infected population. Modeled cascades of care can be used to track progress at regional and global levels. At subnational levels, where the denominator of those with chronic infection may not be available for provinces or districts, or where the catchment area of a healthcare facility is difficult to estimate, the cascade is presented in terms of service delivery data. Various platforms are used to report the cascade of care on program coverage targets. This guidance publication serves as a tool to clarify what is being measured when countries generate cascades depicting the numbers and proportions of individuals with hepatitis C or B who have progressed to diagnosis, treatment, care, and cure. Program officers are encouraged to use this guidance for national monitoring and reporting and to utilize the resulting data for WHO global reporting or validating hepatitis elimination. Reporting should include detailed methods for calculating the cascade of care data, including in government reports and websites. The Monitoring and Evaluation Framework for Viral Hepatitis B and C provides a description of cascade indicators for program reporting. For example, the proportion of individuals with chronic hepatitis B who have been diagnosed is calculated by dividing the number of diagnosed individuals (defined by HBsAg-positive serological status) by the estimated total number of individuals with chronic hepatitis B. Similarly, the proportion of individuals initiating antiviral therapy among those eligible for treatment is calculated. Other indicators include the proportion of individuals currently receiving treatment, the proportion on active follow-up among those not initiating treatment, and the proportion of attrition from antiviral therapy. Person-centered data is critical for organizing health services around the needs and expectations of individuals and communities rather than diseases. Such data supports longitudinal monitoring of clients, including those with hepatitis infections, to improve the quality and continuity of care. Investments in digital health information systems, such as electronic medical records and unique identifiers, have significantly improved data collection, recording, use, and reporting. These systems enhance person-centered patient monitoring and service delivery while improving the quality of aggregated data for surveillance purposes. Person-centered routine data systems are vital sources of strategic information for hepatitis. Analyzing such data provides detailed insights into the characteristics of individuals with hepatitis, the contexts they face, and the underlying factors affecting program outcomes. This enables better decision-making and program improvements. For example, person-centered data can track missed appointments and facilitate follow-up actions, such as sending reminders while respecting client privacy. The use of person-centered data monitoring is essential for the prevention of mother-to-child transmission of hepatitis B, HIV, and syphilis. Eliminating vertical transmission of hepatitis B requires a comprehensive approach, including universal access to the hepatitis B birth-dose vaccine, routine screening of pregnant women, and antiviral prophylaxis or treatment for eligible individuals. Person-centered data can also track HBV-exposed infant-mother pairs to estimate mother-to-child transmission rates. Data on testing uptake, retesting, and testing results is crucial for guiding clinical care and program monitoring, particularly for high-risk populations such as people who inject drugs and immigrant populations. Standardized approaches to data collection across various testing settings and healthcare facilities are necessary to improve care and service delivery. Understanding the reasons for testing in different contexts is critical for interpreting testing indicators and improving data collection and analysis. Finally, linkage to treatment and care is essential for achieving programmatic impact and effective patient management. Person-centered data with unique identifiers strengthens referral systems and ensures continuity of care.
